what_its_for: Tramadol is a pain reliever used to treat moderate to moderately severe pain. Your doctor may prescribe it for pain after surgery, injury, or for ongoing chronic pain conditions.
how_to_take: Take tramadol exactly as your doctor prescribed. You can take it with or without food, but if it upsets your stomach, try taking it with food or milk. Swallow extended-release tablets or capsules whole — do not crush, chew, break, or open them. Only take the dose your doctor told you to take, and never take more than prescribed.
dosing: The typical starting dose for adults is 25 mg once a day in the morning, which may be slowly increased to 50–100 mg every 4 to 6 hours as needed. Do not take more than 400 mg per day. For extended-release forms, the usual dose is 100 mg once daily. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — your dose may be different based on your pain level and health.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never double up or take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store tramadol at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C–25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and light. Store it in a secure location out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused tramadol down the toilet — instead, use a medication take-back program or mix it with an undesirable substance like dirt or coffee grounds, seal it in a bag, and throw it in the trash.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol while taking tramadol — this can cause dangerous side effects, including slowed breathing and even death. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything that requires alertness until you know how tramadol affects you, as it can cause dizziness and drowsiness. Do not take tramadol with other opioid pain medicines, sleeping pills, anti-anxiety medicines, muscle relaxers, or antidepressants without talking to your doctor first. Avoid taking more than prescribed, and never share your medication with others.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: slow, shallow, or stopped breathing; severe dizziness or confusion; seizures; agitation, high fever, sweating, shaking, or fast heart rate (these may be signs of serotonin syndrome); skin rash or allergic reaction; or if you feel your pain is not being controlled. Also contact your doctor if you notice signs of dependence, such as feeling like you need tramadol to function normally or taking more than prescribed.
when_it_works: Tramadol usually starts working within 1 hour after you take a dose. The immediate-release form works for about 4 to 6 hours. The extended-release form is designed to work for 24 hours to give steady pain relief throughout the day. It works best when taken on a regular schedule as directed by your doctor.
special_populations: Older adults (over age 65) should use tramadol with caution, as they may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness and confusion, which can increase the risk of falls. Tramadol should NOT be used in children under 12 years old, and is not recommended for anyone under 18 after certain surgeries. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before taking tramadol — it can harm an unborn baby and pass into breast milk. People with kidney or liver problems may need a lower dose, so always tell your doctor about all your health conditions.
